original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. I did this not only because I had confidence in his taste and his intellect; his opinion was very important to me because, unlike my mother, he had not opposed my wish to become a writer. At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.

MFA.MFA003: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.
MFA.MFA010: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. My domestic circumstances were somewhat fortunate: although my mother believed I could commit myself to more useful professions like law and medicine, my father had always supported my ambition to become a writer. But one memory of my father is more significant than the rest. I remember that when, as a young man, I wrote my first novel, “Cevdet Bay and His Sons,” I sent a copy to my father for his opinion. Till I heard back from him, my days were consumed by the anxiety of what he might have to say. I came to care for my father’s opinion and approval more than anyone else’s. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.
MFA.MFA016: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. Perhaps my father’s support ended now, perhaps I had failed him, perhaps this moment would end this chapter of my life and its purpose. All my anxieties melted when we embraced. He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling me close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride. He held me out in front of him and smiled. “You will succeed, my son,” he said. “You will win prestigious prizes and teach somewhere.” It is this memory I cling to after his death in 2002—how he remained such a father to me.

AI.Claude3.5Sonnet: On that spring evening in Istanbul, when the Bosphorus was painted in shades of amber and violet, I handed my father the manuscript of "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" with trembling hands that betrayed both hope and terror. The pages, worn from countless revisions and bearing the weight of my artistic ambitions, disappeared into his leather briefcase – the same briefcase I had watched him carry to his office countless times throughout my childhood. In the days that followed, I wandered the streets of Nişantaşı like a guilty man, examining the faces of passersby as if they might offer some preview of my father's judgment. Unlike my mother, who had always viewed my literary aspirations with the kind of worried skepticism reserved for a child's dangerous games, my father had maintained a curious silence about my choice to abandon architecture for the solitary life of a novelist. I remember sitting in the old Pamuk Apartments, listening to the distant ferry horns and watching the dust particles dance in the afternoon light that filtered through the heavy curtains, wondering if I had disappointed him. When he finally returned home that evening, before any words could form between us, he embraced me with an intensity that spoke volumes in our family's language of unspoken emotions. Later, as we sat in his study surrounded by his beloved books – the ones that had first taught me to love literature – he broke our emotional silence with words that would echo through the decades: "You will win great prizes one day." That moment hung between us like a photograph yellowing with age, gaining new meaning after his death in 2002, when I found myself standing alone in that same study, running my fingers along the spines of his books, feeling the weight of his absence and the enduring power of his belief in me.
AI.Gemini_1.5_Pro: The weight of the manuscript, a physical embodiment of years of creative struggle, felt familiar and foreign in my hands.  I had poured my heart and soul into "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," a tale woven from the rich tapestry of Istanbul's history and the intricate lives of its inhabitants.  The city, my muse and my prison, had borne witness to my solitary journey as a writer, a path I had chosen despite the uncertainties that gnawed at my soul.My father, unlike my mother, had always encouraged my artistic pursuits, seeing in them a reflection of his own unfulfilled dreams.  He had been a source of quiet strength, a steady hand on my shoulder as I navigated the treacherous waters of self-expression.  His return from Paris, a city that had both beckoned and betrayed him, had been a turning point in our relationship.The silence that followed my presentation of the manuscript was thick with unspoken emotions.  My father's embrace, a gesture of paternal affection and unspoken approval, had eased the anxieties that had plagued me for years.  His words, when they finally came, were filled with a conviction that surprised and humbled me."You will win the Nobel Prize one day," he had declared, his voice echoing with a certainty that transcended the boundaries of fatherly pride.The memory of that moment, etched into the deepest recesses of my mind, had become a source of solace and inspiration in the years that followed.  My father's belief in my abilities, his unwavering support for my artistic ambitions, had sustained me through the inevitable doubts and setbacks that litter the path of any creative endeavor.Even now, years after his passing in 2002, the echo of his words continues to resonate within me, a reminder of the enduring power of familial love and the transformative potential of artistic expression.
AI.GPT4: I remember the moment I handed over my first novel, "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," to my father as if it were encased in amber, frozen in a delicate yet trembling moment of time. In the quiet of our Istanbul apartment, the weight of the manuscript in my hands mirrored the gravity of the step I was about to take. My mother, though ever loving, had dismissed my ambitions as mere indulgence, a detour from the secure path she imagined for me. My father, however, had always encouraged the flickering flame of my aspirations. He took the manuscript with an easy, almost playful smile, as though we were conspirators in some artistic rebellion. When he returned, his embrace was not rushed or obligatory—it was deliberate, a gesture heavy with the unspoken weight of approval. It was as if he had passed a verdict, not only on the book but on the very path I had chosen for my life. He didn’t speak immediately; instead, he held me, his silence filled with a fatherly pride that words might have diminished. Then, in a voice steadied by conviction, he said I would succeed and even prophesied a prestigious prize in my future. The precision of his faith startled me—how could he be so sure when I wasn’t? This memory, so vivid and immutable, grew to anchor me, particularly after his death in 2002. It is strange how the weight of approval from someone who is no longer there can linger like a ghost in the room, shaping the contours of your own self-belief. My father’s prediction, his prophecy of my future success, stands as a monument to his faith in me, a beacon amidst the ever-shifting uncertainties of life and art.

GPT4_Finetuned: Thirty years ago, my father gave me a small suitcase like the one in this image, filled with his manuscripts, and asked me to read them. I held that suitcase in my hand for a full week, imagining its contents and wavering between the melancholy solitude it would bring and my desire not to disappoint my father. Finally, I decided not to open it because I wanted to remain the child of a father who kept a suitcase of secrets. When my first novel "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" was published in Turkey, I was twenty-three, and I gave it to my father to read. Until then, I had never given him any samples of my writing, and that small suitcase had not yet been mentioned between us. Unlike my mother, my father—who was concerned for my welfare but even more for my freedom—did not object to my becoming a novelist. Like all fathers, he wished for his son to have extraordinary success, yet he refrained from making demands, urging me only to be free and happy.I waited, as nervous as my mother was, for my father's reaction after he had finished reading my novel. Finally, when he returned, overcome with excitement, I studied his expression and searched for clues. My father said not a word, but—ignoring my mother and the others—motioned for me to follow him into his study. For a time, we stood across from each other, like two schoolboys who had quarreled, awkwardly unable to speak. Then, embarrassed by his own emotions, he hugged me. When we pulled apart, he looked at me affectionately and said, "You will be a very good writer, bebeğim." He then added, like a true man of his generation, that he expected me to one day win the prize I am receiving today. I recount this here proudly, yet with some embarrassment—and his supposition has come true.My dear father died in December 2002.

original: My mother had a bachelor cousin a good deal younger than her, who used to visit us on the farm every summer. He brought along his mother, Aunt Nell Botts. His own name was Ernie Botts. He was a tall, florid man with a good-natured expression, a big square face, and fair curly hair springing straight up from his forehead. His hands, his fingernails were as clean as soap itself; his hips were a little plump. My name for him—when he was not around—was Earnest Bottom. I had a mean tongue.But I meant no harm. Or hardly any harm.After Aunt Nell Botts died Ernie did not come to visit anymore, but he always sent a Christmas card.When I started college in the city where he lived, he began a custom of taking me out to dinner every other Sunday evening. He did this because I was a relative—it’s unlikely that he even considered whether we were suited to spending time together. He always took me to the same place, a restaurant called the Old Chelsea, which was on the second floor of a building, looking down on Dundas Street. It had velvet curtains, white tablecloths, little rose-shaded lamps on the tables. It probably cost more, strictly speaking, than he could afford, but I did not think of that, having a country girl’s notion that all men who lived in the city, wore a suit every day, and sported such clean fingernails had reached a level of prosperity where indulgences like this were a matter of course.

MFA.MFA033: Ernie Botts. Ernie. My younger cousin, who was to remain a lifelong bachelor, had once spent each summer with us on the farm, showing up shyly in tow that first season in the shadow of my Aunt Nell. I hadn’t liked having to share a room with my sister, as I did when he came to visit. But he made up for it, with his good-natured affability, and his curious habit of punctilious grooming. I’d had the idea to call him Earnest Bottom-and my use of this nickname behind his back brought my sister and myself no end of amusement. The visits stopped when Aunt Nell passed, Ernie then thirteen. His presence in our house dwindled to a card each Christmas in his spidery handwriting. At eighteen I took the train out to the city, planning to start university at last and my new life. That my cousin lived there too was the last thing on my mind. It was my mother who reminded me. She told me I should look him up, conjuring at once his easy, slightly high-pitched laugh, his perfectly brushed wool sweaters. From then, Ernie and I had dinner every other Sunday, at a place called the Old Chelsea. I wasn’t sure why. I couldn’t tell if he had real fondness for me. His old habits of grooming were accompanied now by a certain formality of speech. It wasn’t a cheap restaurant either, but one of those old-style, stiff tablecloth establishments that used to be in vogue then. We always had three courses and wine. I assumed his loyalty to the Old Chelsea, and to me, meant he could easily afford such luxuries.
MFA.MFA025: Aunt Nell used to tote Cousin Ernie Botts to the farm every summer like he was an old handbag or umbrella. He never seemed to mind, smiling banally to show off his fantastic straight, white teeth. He was a clean boy, a good boy, so much so that in the privacy of my own mind, I called him Earnest Bottom. When Aunt Nell passed, there was no one to drag sweet Ernie around, so we stopped seeing him for a while. Mother made sure to send him Christmas cards every year, and I’d doodle him little flowers and rainbows on the back. After I was accepted into college, I wrote him a little note instead, telling him I’d be moving to his city. He wrote back saying we really ought to get dinner once I was settled. We did, and it morphed into an every-other-Sunday affair. Ernie would pick me up at my dorm and drive me to a charming little restaurant called the Old Chelsea. Ernie insisted on us ordering two appetizers each, a main course, dessert, and of course, an after-dinner coffee. The checks, when I managed to glimpse them, always made my eyes bug. But Ernie was a good person, and the elaborate dinners never seemed to me a desire to show off, but rather a way to remain a part of the family. If he could spend so confidently every other week, I presumed he was working one of those legitimate office jobs. He never did talk all that much about himself.
MFA.MFA029: It is impossible to think of the Old Chelsea without thinking, too, of Earnest Bottom. His real name, of course, was Ernie Botts—my slightly younger and far more sophisticated cousin. We'd spent many summers together as children at my family's farm. Ernie was prim and manicured and always seemed to be dusting off his pants or scraping mud from the soles of his shoes. At Aunt Nell's funeral, he shook everyone's hands in his freshly pressed suit and thanked them for the flowers. He stopped coming to the farm after that, but we kept in touch through Christmas cards, which he always signed with a kind, personalized note. Our paths ran perpendicular again when I went to graduate school in his city. As soon as he heard I was in town, he locked me into his calendar for dinner every other Sunday. The Old Chelsea had an excellent fillet mignon, he told me, and it was true. The food offset the conversation, which was stale at best. Talk of work and school died out quickly, and I felt guilty talking about my social life—while I was making friends and had started going steady with a classmate, Ernie seemed to be suspended in self-imposed monkhood. Somehow, the bill always ended up in Ernie's hands. “It’s the least I can do,” he’d say, batting away the money I offered, and I couldn’t help but wonder what he thought he owed me.

AI.Claude3.5Sonnet: Ernie Botts—whom I privately called "Earnest Bottom" in those days of ruthless teenage cleverness—would arrive at our farm each summer with Aunt Nell, his clothes pressed and his hair neatly combed, as if the three-hour drive on dusty country roads had somehow failed to touch him. He had that particular quality of bachelor sons, a kind of pristine wholesomeness that spoke of carefully maintained routines and unspoken maternal guidance. After Aunt Nell died (a quick death, heart attack while hanging laundry), the summer visits stopped, though Christmas cards arrived without fail, bearing generic winter scenes and his meticulously penned signature. Years later, when I started college in his city, he began taking me to dinner at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday—a restaurant with heavy maroon drapes and waiters who wore black bow ties with an air of weary dignity. I suspected these dinners cost more than he should have spent, but there was something both touching and slightly oppressive about his insistence on maintaining this connection, as if he were fulfilling some deathbed promise to Aunt Nell that I'd never been told about. I assumed he could afford it; after all, he lived in an apartment building with a doorman and wore suits that looked expensive in their subtle way. But sometimes I'd catch him studying the menu with a carefully blank expression, and I'd remember how Aunt Nell used to darken last year's coat with shoe polish to make it look new. There are some kinds of family duty that run deeper than affection, I suppose, though I never quite knew which one brought Ernie to that restaurant every other Sunday, in his good suit, precisely on time.
AI.Gemini_1.5_Pro: Ernie Botts—Earnest Bottom, as I’d christened him in the foolish privacy of my head—was the clean and well-groomed sort of boy my mother admired.  He was always neat, pressed, and polite, the kind who’d never show up with grass stains or a ripped shirt.  Each summer, he’d arrive at our farm with his mother, Aunt Nell, a high-pitched echo of my mother’s pronouncements on how a young man ought to behave.  After Aunt Nell passed, the summer visits stopped, replaced by the steady arrival of Christmas cards—always signed “Ernie,” never the “Earnest Bottom” of my childhood.    Years later, when I found myself in his city for college, Ernie took it upon himself to take me out to dinner every other Sunday.  The Old Chelsea, the restaurant he chose, was the kind of place with heavy silverware and hushed conversations, the sort of place I figured Ernie frequented—though how a bachelor school teacher could afford it, I didn’t know.  Perhaps I’d underestimated a school teacher’s salary, or perhaps, like the old aunts I’d left back home, he’d scrimped and saved for the sake of appearances.  Ernie wasn’t much of a conversationalist, and I often found myself making idle chatter, filling the silences between his polite inquiries about my studies and his pronouncements on the weather.  I figured it was family duty that brought him, not any real desire for my company.  Still, there was something amusing about being seen in such a place with a man like Ernie—Earnest Bottom, the clean-cut boy turned proper bachelor.
AI.GPT4o: During those summers on the farm, Ernie Botts, who we’d mischievously dubbed “Earnest Bottom,” became a predictable part of the season, like the first crop of sweet corn or the relentless hum of cicadas. He was always impeccably groomed—his blond hair neatly combed, his fingernails somehow untouched by dirt, even after a day spent traipsing through the fields. He was good-natured in a way that set him apart from the brashness of other cousins who fought over fishing rods or snickered at Aunt Nell’s awkward manners. Ernie simply smiled and carried on, often humming quietly as he helped with chores or indulged my younger siblings by playing checkers on the front porch. When Aunt Nell passed away, his visits ended, replaced only by his dutiful Christmas cards that seemed to grow shorter with each year. By the time I moved to his city for college, he was a figure shrouded in distant nostalgia, though he reappeared with an almost rehearsed sincerity, treating me to dinners at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday. The crisp white napkins, the polite waitstaff, the gleaming wine glasses—it all seemed to mirror Ernie himself, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that these outings were more about obligation than genuine kinship. But still, I didn’t protest. His generosity, even if tinged with a faint remoteness, filled the silences left by years and miles, a duty performed with meticulous care and quiet resolve.

original: There was old sex in the room and loneliness, and expectation, of something without a shape or name. I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.

MFA.MFA029: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.
MFA.MFA004: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.
MFA.MFA008: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We want to move, but we are afraid of the cattle prods, because we have seen what they do to others, the way bodies twist under them like writhing serpents, the way skin burns where the prods touched them for days after. We watch the Angels, too, guards who gaze into the distance as though they are somewhere else, far away. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine a world where we beg for our freedom, for the chance to go outside, into the egg-colored sun, to step barefoot on the wet grass, to spin in the cool wind of the day. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. But we know better than to go to them. They are the ones with loaded guns, which they hold cradled in their arms like babies. We’ve seen what has happened to the girls who dare to speak to the Angels, the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.

AI.Claude3.5Sonnet: We are watched. Always watched, but never truly seen. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrol the corridors with their cattle prods held like scepters, symbols of their petty authority, though it's the Angels outside who hold the real power, with their guns and their untouchable distance. I've memorized the way they stand, these Angels, their backs military-straight against the concrete walls, their eyes hidden beneath the peaks of their caps. Sometimes I imagine their gaze following me, and I let my hips sway ever so slightly – an old habit from before, when such movements held currency. Now they're just muscle memory, like the way my hands still reach for a phone that isn't there, or my fingers itch for a cigarette I can't have. The other women do it too; I see them in the cafeteria, in the exercise yard, their bodies unconsciously remembering freedom. We're like cats in a cage, I think, practicing our hunting crouch though there's nothing left to hunt. At night, in our narrow beds, we whisper about making deals – our bodies for their help, as if we still owned these vessels we inhabit. As if flesh could buy freedom in a place where flesh is all we're reduced to. The routine grinds on: wake, pray, eat, walk, pray, sleep. The cold seeps in through the windows, but it's nothing compared to the chill that's settled in our bones. We are learning to fold ourselves smaller, to take up less space, to become invisible even as we're constantly observed. Yet somewhere, in the midnight hours when even Aunt Sara's footsteps fade, we dream of tomorrow, of a future that feels as distant and unreachable as the stars beyond our barred windows.
AI.Gemini_1.5_Pro: The yearning within me is like a phantom limb, a constant ache for something I cannot name.  It is a thirst for touch, for freedom, for the scent of rain on soil.  But these desires are forbidden, locked away in the depths of our sterile existence. Aunt Sara and Elizabeth, the keepers of our gilded cage, watch with hawk-like eyes, their cattle prods a silent threat.  They are the keepers of our morality, the guardians of our chastity.  Their voices echo in the cold, sterile corridors, a constant reminder of our confinement. The Angels, those distant figures in their pristine uniforms, are the only ones permitted to bear arms.  They are the true power in this desolate realm, the enforcers of our isolation.  We crave their attention, their touch, their recognition.  Our bodies, the only currency we possess, become our bargaining chips in silent negotiations.The days bleed into one another, an endless cycle of rituals and routines.  The cold, impersonal walls of this place mirror the chill that has settled deep within our bones.  We are cogs in a machine, our individuality erased, our voices muted.Yet, beneath the surface of our resignation, a spark of rebellion flickers. original: One evening ‒ it was our last day ‒ in Tours, we had dinner in a brightly-lit restaurant where the walls were lined with mirrors, frequented by a sophisticated clientele. My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. She was dipping into a thick milky substance in a glass ‒ some years later I learnt this was yogurt, which people like us had never heard of. I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad-looking with my spectacles, silently sitting beside my father, who was staring into the far distance. I could see everything that separated me from that girl yet I wouldn’t have known what to do to resemble her.Afterward, my father complained with unusual vehemence about this restaurant, where he claimed we had been served mashed potatoes made with “pig slop,” white and tasteless. Several weeks later, he was still venting his anger over the meal and its disgraceful “pig slop.” Although he never actually said so ‒ it was probably then that I began decoding his speech ‒ it was his way of expressing resentment at having been treated with contempt because we were not chic customers who ate “à la carte.”

MFA.MFA016: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
MFA.MFA011: My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food. It was clear that both of us felt uncomfortable with the opulence of the space, but neither of us knew how to say so. Nearby, a girl around the age of fifteen sat with an older man, presumably her father, eating a foreign-looking food that I didn't recognize—a bowl of yogurt, I later learned. She looked deeply at ease eating her meal, and I was disturbed to see myself in the mirror on the adjacent wall—spectacled, pale. Compared to the girl, I looked homely and unimportant, or at least I felt that I did at the time. For a moment I imagined myself as the girl, tan and comfortable among the trappings of wealth, though even then I knew that the hallmarks of the working class were written all over my face and my behavior. My father and I sat for a while in silence, and when the waitstaff brought out our plates, he remarked to me that his mashed potatoes looked like "pig slop." At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.
MFA.MFA033: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately. I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion, the kind you could buy at a steep discount. The waiter directed us to a shared table at the back of the restaurant, in front of the wash closet. At first my experience of discomfort was limited only to me. My father still had a big smile, ear to ear. But then I saw another father-daughter pair at a table in the restaurant’s big window. The girl was around my age, and pretty. She dealt with the restaurant staff confidently, with a confiding air, like they shared a special secret. I watched the girl longingly. Her tanned legs ended in delicate buckled shoes. I watched her eat food I could not identify. Back then, I’d never had yoghurt.As the waiter laughed and spoke to them in earshot of us, I saw my father growing red. “Those potatoes were pig slop,” he said after we left the restaurant, again and again. It embarrassed me. It was clear enough to both of us what had happened. At least, it was clear that we’d both had a bad time. I knew what he was saying. We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele. I wanted to forget about it. If we didn’t speak of the event, then perhaps it wasn’t real.

original: I watched my mother. It was March, and outside, the sun glinted off the sidewalks and the icy edges of the snow. It was Saint Patrick’s Day and the nurses brought my mother a square block of green Jell-O that sat quivering on the table beside her. It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open. They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake. They were the color of the sky on the best day of your life.My mother died fast but not all of a sudden. A slow-burning fire when flames disappear to smoke and then smoke to air. She never once closed her eyes. First they were bitter and then they were bewildered and then they changed again to something else, to a state that I have had, finally, to see as heroic. Blue, blue eyes. Daggers of blue wanting and wanting. To stay, to stay.

MFA.MFA009: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?

original: Many of the houses that looked abandoned were occupied, by Africans who had come in from the forest and had used the awkward, angular objects they had found, walls, doors, windows, furniture, to re-create the shelter of the round forest hut. Within drawing-rooms they had built shelters; they had raised roofs on verandah half-walls. Fires burned on pieces of corrugated iron; bricks were the cooking stones. On the sidewalks grass had grown around rubbish from the houses, things that couldn’t be used and had been thrown out: cracked squares of picture glass, fragments of upholstered chairs, mattresses that had been disembowelled for their springs, books and magazines whose pages had stuck together in solid, crinkled pads. Once Bobby saw a flattened cigarette packet, black on faded red: Belga. It recalled European holidays: as though Belgium and Europe had once lain across the water, and the lake had only been a version of the English Channel. This resort hadn’t been built for tourists in Africa; it had been created by people who thought they had come to Africa to stay, and looked in a resort for a version of the things of home: a park, a pier, a waterside promenade. Now, after the troubles across the lake, after independence and the property scare, after the army mutiny, after the white exodus South and the Asian deportations, after all these deaths, the resort no longer had a function.

But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." And so the empty building sat, bludgeoned by the naked sun, waiting again for peace, for purpose.
MFA.MFA032: The forecourt wore it well—time, and the fickle seasons of democracy in this place. The moldings decorating the façade betrayed nothing either, except perhaps the usual negligence, the fine patina of dust that came over everything in Africa. But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.

original: Much later, after she had left her husband and lived several years with Jean-Marc, she was at the seashore one day: they were dining outdoors, on a wooden deck over the water; she retains an intense memory of whiteness: the deck, the tables, the chairs, the tablecloths, everything was white, the lampposts were painted white and the bulbs beamed a white light against the summer sky, not yet dark, where the moon, itself white too, was whitening everything around them. And in this bath of white she was struck by a feeling of unbearable nostalgia for Jean-Marc. Nostalgia? How could she feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her? How can you suffer from the absence of a person who is present? (Jean-Marc knew how to answer that: you can suffer nostalgia in the presence of the beloved if you glimpse a future where the beloved is no more; if the beloved’s death is, invisibly, already present.) During that moment of strange nostalgia at the seaside, she suddenly thought of her dead child, and a wave of happiness flooded over her. Soon she would be frightened by this feeling. But no one can do a thing about feelings, they exist and there’s no way to censor them. We can reproach ourselves for some action, for a remark, but not for a feeling, quite simply because we have no control at all over it.

She thought the feeling meant: life will never get better than this. The future was her and Jean-Marc, together, but older, and recovered from the mania of fresh love, or perhaps not together at all. But how is it apprpropriate to feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her ? (Jean-Marc however had the answer: the more intensely we love someone in the present, the more we grieve their inevitable absence in some imagined future.) But she did not think that was what she meant at all! The mention of death made her think of the child. The child, forever a child, existing without complication in her death. The solidity of this shot her through with pure happiness. She felt afraid; she clasped her hands together in her lap and said nothing more. How easy it is to reign in our words and actions! But then there is always feeling, loping around like an untrained dog inside all of us, aware of how much we long to leash it.
MFA.MFA018: When she imagined this moment months ago, lying beside her husband, she had pictured herself happy. So why wasn't she? It suddenly struck her that everything in the seaside restaurant was white: the deck, the table, the lampposts. Even the moon, stark and full, shone unbearably white tonight. Jean-Marc asked: "What is the matter with you, my dear? You are so quiet tonight." "Nothing really," she said, knowing it was a lie. Something was wrong, but she could not put that something into words. It was a strange yet acute longing for what was already hers, sitting right there in front of her. Jean-Marc, feeling the melancholy in the air, said: "Nostalgia comes from the fear of losing someone and imagining life without them." She thought of her child, the only person she had truly lost. The memory struck her with unexpected happiness, followed immediately by fear. What did it mean to feel sadness at dinner with her lover but happiness thinking of her dead child? Was there something wrong with her? Was she a bad mother, a bad person? Not according to Scottish philosopher David Hume. Hume had argued emotions were natural and involuntary. While we could control our actions, we could never control our feelings.

Fine particles of garlic, onion, and olive oil swirled in the air, forming a harmonious cloud that penetrated every corner of my tiny apartment, permeating the floor and the ceiling and the walls, my clothes, my books, my records, my tennis racquet, my bundles of old letters. It was a fragrance one might have smelled on ancient Roman aqueducts.This is a story from the Year of Spaghetti, 1971 A.D.As a rule, I cooked spaghetti, and ate it, by myself. I was convinced that spaghetti was a dish best enjoyed alone. I can’t really explain why I felt that way, but there it is.I always drank tea with my spaghetti and ate a simple lettuce-and-cucumber salad. I’d make sure I had plenty of both. I laid everything out neatly on the table and enjoyed a leisurely meal, glancing at the paper as I ate. From Sunday to Saturday, one Spaghetti Day followed another. And each new Sunday started a brand-new Spaghetti Week

I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. original: It was early winter, the first frost of the year. My 22-year-old mother crawled into the kitchen and boiled some water to sterilise a pair of scissors. Fumbling in her sewing box, she found some white cloth that would do for a newborn’s gown. Gripped by contractions and terribly afraid, tears started down as she plied her needle. She finished the tiny gown, found a thin quilt to use as swaddling bands, and gritted her teeth as the pain returned, quicker and more intense each time.Eventually, she gave birth. Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord. She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. For god’s sake don’t die, she muttered in a thin voice, over and over like a mantra. After an hour had passed, the baby’s tight-sealed eyelids abruptly unseamed. As my mother’s eyes encountered those of her child, her lips twitched again. For god’s sake don’t die. Around an hour later, the baby was dead. They lay there on the kitchen floor, my mother on her side with the dead baby clutched to her chest, feeling the cold gradually leach into the flesh, sinking through to the bone. No more crying.

MFA.MFA011: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.
MFA.MFA025: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.
MFA.MFA010: The early days of winter remind my mother of her dead child. My father knew that my mother was due at any moment, but the roads were icy and the entire landscape had turned bare and hostile, preventing him from returning home.My mother was in labor, all by herself at home, and the ripples of her screams were absorbed by the walls, making cracks that had not existed before. In the kitchen, she tried as best as she could. She kept some water to boil in a small pot to sterilize a pair of kitchen scissors. She took off her clothes and quickly fashioned a hospital gown from some fabric that was guarded in a sewing box.Gripped by fear and pain so intense that she felt larger and more forceful than the dazzle of winter outside, my mother held a baby—slippery and blood-covered—in her arms. She had pushed and pushed, and had severed the umbilical cord with the hot pair of scissors that had burned her fingers. She chanted an old prayer, a common plea for life, but felt the warmth of the baby's body fading.My mother tells me that is when she stopped screaming. In a fleeting moment, the alchemy of the house shifted: life became death. The coldness of the floor seeped through her own body. It became impossible to tell whether the air was so still because of the cold, or her grief, or both.

original: She was beautiful and lithe, with soft skin the color of bread and eyes like green almonds, and she had straight black hair that reached to her shoulders, and an aura of antiquity that could just as well have been Indonesian as Andean. She was dressed with subtle taste: a lynx jacket, a raw silk blouse with very delicate flowers, natural linen trousers, and shoes with a narrow stripe the color of bougainvillea. ‘This is the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen,’ I thought, when I saw her pass by with the stealthy stride of a lioness, while I waited in the check-in line at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris for the plane to New York.She was a supernatural apparition who existed only for a moment and disappeared into the crowd in the terminal.It was nine in the morning. It had been snowing all night, and traffic was heavier than usual in the city streets, and even slower on the highway, where trailer trucks were lined up on the shoulder and automobiles steamed in the snow. Inside the airport terminal, however, it was still spring.I stood behind an old Dutch woman who spent almost an hour arguing about the weight of her eleven suitcases. I was beginning to feel bored when I saw the momentary apparition who left me breathless, and so I never knew how the dispute ended. Then the ticket clerk brought me down from the clouds with a reproach for my distraction. By way of an excuse, I asked her if she believed in love at first sight. "Of course," she said. "The other kinds are impossible."

MFA.MFA026: In Paris I spotted her walking gracefully in short suede heels, a timeless click to her step on the shiny floors of the Charles de Gaulle Airport. She was magnificent, her limbs like tributaries each meeting at the river made by her dark and wavy hair. Her eyes, though I could not see them, were certainly slant and blue. Fortuitously she sat some feet away from where I stood in line at the counter, crossing her ankles neatly beneath her in the French way, and at last I could admire a charoite skirt and matching cinched blazer that met the milky skin at her thighs and neck. The whole of her became a river to me then, or perhaps instead a lioness paused to drink at cool water; soon, I knew, she would be gone, and the springtime warmth and vibrancy brought by her into this terminal would fade to match the great blank whiteness of snowy winter beyond our shared space. Infatuated as I was by this lion-headed goddess, it took me some time to process the bickering before me, an elderly woman with a thick Dutch accent and some eleven suitcases haggling with the ticket clerk over their weight and associated cost. Returning my attention to the woman cloaked in purple and, for the time being, likewise cloaked in the wholeness of my affection, I missed the ticket clerk calling me forward after the Dutch woman had been sorted. I smiled a wide and generous smile. “Do you believe love at first sight is impossible,” I asked him, and tilted my head gently so that he might see the object of my sighted love.The clerk, evidently harried, was still inspired to smile at the glimpse of an exceptional woman. “In Paris,” he told me, “Anything other than such a love is impossible.”
MFA.MFA016: I stood in line with my luggage at the Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris when my eyes landed on the most striking woman in the building, perhaps the most striking woman I’d ever seen; her pearly skin, antiquated dress and golden eyes gave her the aura of a masquerading goddess who’d absconded from her oil painting. The cardigan draped around her neck popped with magenta zags and her gold necklace turned the bleachy overhead lights to warm shine. With the grace of a lioness, she stepped out of sight and I lost her. I waited for my chance to pursue her down the terminal hall, but an elderly Dutch woman haggled with the clerk in front of me, producing short vehement barks about the weight of her eleven suitcases. There was time to plan. I looked around for an avenue for conversation with the beauty ahead, assuming I might never catch her, and found myself gazing at the snow falling like ash outside, silent out there, a perfect contrast to the balmy and chatty world inside the terminal. I edged around the Dutchwoman and her astonishing pile of luggage, which could easily fill a cargo barge, hoping for another glimpse of the leoline woman. There she went, distant now, turning left at the junction down the hall, heading in the same direction I soon would--there was still a chance. “Is love at first sight possible?” I asked the clerk when my turn came. He smiled. “Anything else is impossible,” he replied.
MFA.MFA011: Walking into Charles de Gaulle Airport, I saw a woman, exotic and striking in her beauty. Astonished, I stood frozen in the terminal as I gazed at her timeless features. Her skin was dark and glowed with youth, her eyes were clear as a glacial lake. She wore a garment of gold and red fabric that looked as though it came from a culture that was entirely unfamiliar to me, and I stood for a long time admiring it, as though in a trance. Her look suggested an aura of antiquity, and she moved in grace like a lioness, striding confidently across the bright, balmy terminal that contrasted with the snowy world beyond its walls. In a moment, she was gone, her presence as fleeting as it was alluring. I took my place in line, and for a moment I found myself distracted by an elderly Dutch woman who took it upon herself to argue with the ticket clerk about the weight of eleven suitcases, “I’ve weighed them at home,” she said, “they can’t possibly be more than 10 kilograms—” and by the time I reached the front of the line I found myself in a pensive and dreamy mood. Who was that woman of such incredible mystery and poise, whose eyes shone so brightly? Smiling, I asked the ticket clerk if he believed in love at first sight. He laughed and replied that of course he did, how could he not. "Anything short of this , would be impossible", the clerk said.

She moved through Terminal 2F with the deliberate grace of a lioness, her caftan catching whispers of air that seemed to carry the scent of frankincense and myrrh, though later I would learn it was nothing more than the perfume of duty-free shops mixing with the aroma of croissants from Paul's bakery. Her eyes, set like amber stones in an Ethiopian crown, caught the fluorescent lights in such a way that made me believe she had lived a thousand years, perhaps more, and had witnessed the rise and fall of civilizations that existed only in forgotten dreams. The snow outside fell with the determination of white butterflies against the glass walls, while inside, the terminal maintained its eternal springtime, as if nature herself had conceded to this woman's presence. I might have followed her forever through the labyrinth of gates and shops, but fate, with its peculiar sense of humor, placed me behind an elderly Dutch woman who carried eleven suitcases and argued with mathematical precision about each gram of their weight, her voice rising and falling like a baroque opera. When I finally reached the ticket counter, my head still swimming with visions of the mysterious woman, I asked the clerk, a man with a mustache that seemed to have been drawn by a child's uncertain hand, if he believed in love at first sight. "Monsieur," he replied, adjusting his tie with the gravity of a philosopher, "in this airport, the only impossible thing is to find a reasonable price for a cup of coffee."

original: There was a crime. But there were also the lovers. Lovers and their happy ends have been on my mind all night long. As into the sunset we sail. An unhappy inversion. It occurs to me that I have not traveled so very far after all, since I wrote my little play. Or rather, I’ve made a huge digression and doubled back to my starting place. It is only in this last version that my lovers end well, standing side by side on a South London pavement as I walk away. All the preceding drafts were pitiless. But now I can no longer think what purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on 1 June 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station. That I never saw them in that year. That my walk across London ended at the church on Clapham Common, and that a cowardly Briony limped back to the hospital, unable to confront her recently bereaved sister. That the letters the lovers wrote are in the archives of the War Museum. How could that constitute an ending? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love?

MFA.MFA008: Robbie and Cecilia were happy in my story. They faced hardships, certainly, but I conjured them, by the force of my own brittle pen, into two happy people. The world, the real world, was not as kind to them. I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.
MFA.MFA029: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.
MFA.MFA025: The truth is much uglier than the sweet story I’ve given them. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis never saw each other again, both having perished during the war. Robbie fell to septicemia at Bray Dunes, his wounds never healing right. Cecilia, my glamorous older sister, died in a bombing at the Balham Underground, dressed in the same rationed rags as any other woman. They died alone, a fault I must now agonizingly take the blame for. It was my callous childishness that ripped Robbie from Cecilia, but it is my better nature that has prompted me to write them a better ending. They find each other again, they live, and they are happy. What good would it do, I beg to know, in telling the foul truth? I’ll tell it, here and now, if only to prove my point. I never saw either of them again that year, how could I, after what I had done to Cecilia? Their love died with them, isolated and unfulfilled, with the sole evidence that they knew each other being those romantic letters preserved only in a war museum. I cannot imagine truth is worth more than the merciful fiction, but I struggle even now to know for certain if my rewrite of history is fair. I’d like to think that this hopeful conclusion, regardless of how factual it may be, holds greater value than an honest, but tragic account.

AI.Claude3.5Sonnet: Truth sits heavily in my hands like an old manuscript, its pages yellow and brittle with time. I could write it all - the harsh reality of their separate deaths, Robbie's slow fade into septicemic darkness at Bray Dunes, Cecilia's final moments in the underground station at Balham, their love scattered like ash across a war-torn continent. The historian in me demands this accuracy, this unflinching record of what actually transpired after my childish testimony tore them apart. But what serves memory better - the brutal facts preserved in glass cases at the Imperial War Museum, those letters never to be answered, those promises never to be kept, or the mercy of imagination that allows them to transcend the circumstances I thrust upon them? In my fiction, they live. In my fiction, their hands find each other across the library table, their eyes meet without the shadow of my betrayal between them. Perhaps this is my final act of cowardice, unable even now to face the full weight of what I did, unable to write the words that would kill them again on the page. Or perhaps it is the only grace left to me - this power to resurrect them from the ashes of history, to give them the moments that war and my testimony stole. The question haunts me: is truth always kinder than fiction? In the end, I choose to let them live in the amber of my imagination, preserved in a love that reality never permitted them to fully express.
AI.Gemini_1.5_Pro: The lingering image of Robbie and Cecilia, their figures receding down the driveway into the white mist, remains etched in my memory. It's a scene I've revisited countless times, a reminder of the love I shattered and the atonement I sought through my writing. In the twilight of my life, I question the nature of truth. Is a merciful fabrication, a crafted illusion of happiness, a greater kindness than the stark reality of a love tragically cut short? Robbie likely succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes. Cecilia perished in Balham Underground station during a bombing raid. Their letters lie preserved in a war museum, a testament to a love forever unfulfilled. Yet, in my final act of creation, I dared to defy fate. I granted them a reprieve, a fictional sanctuary where their love survived. It was a rebellion against the relentless march of time and tragedy. As the shadows lengthen, I wonder if I was right to weave this tapestry of hope. Would they have preferred the stark truth, the bitter knowledge of their unfulfilled love? Or is it a greater kindness to let them live on in my fictional world, forever young, forever in love? The question lingers, unresolved, like an echo in my mind. Perhaps there is no right answer to this age-old dilemma. Perhaps the truth, like beauty, lies in the eye of the beholder. A hopeful ending, even if untrue, is a more fitting tribute to their love than the harsh reality of their tragic fate.
AI.GPT4o: In the twilight of her long life, Briony Tallis grappled with the burden of her narrative. Her pages were a desperate reach for atonement, a reckoning with a truth too cruel to bear. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis had never enjoyed the solace of a country retreat or the satisfaction of a love realized. The world had not been kind enough to allow their survival. Yet in the theater of her imagination, Briony became their savior, conjuring them together, their lives intact, their love unbroken, their letters exchanged with trembling hands. The truth, stark and unrelenting, loomed like the specter of her own guilt: Robbie felled by infection in the mud-soaked trenches, Cecilia extinguished in a cataclysm of rubble and fire. She, the architect of their suffering, could not face the permanence of that ending. What then was the purpose of truth, she wondered, if it could not redeem? In her constructed fiction, she gave them joy, continuity, the soft rebellion of a life shared. But as the ink dried on her final pages, she was left with the echo of a question that gnawed at her sense of justice and her fragile hope for forgiveness: was it better to honor the brutal finality of fact or to bestow upon them, and herself, the balm of a beautiful lie? GPT4_Finetuned: I'm rounding off this untidy decade, meeting my deadline, and choosing to let my lovers live and unite them at the end. I want to give Robbie and Cecilia what they lost out on in life. They both died because of a simple mistake which, although it grew in significance over the years, was not difficult to expunge. Hypocrites—I needed their praise and confirmation, and my sisters' doubts and contempt, in order to be cured. But now I must sleep. I will close my eyes and sleep. What purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on June 1, 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station? original: One Saturday morning, the man who had actually killed the former premier went to his dead uncle’s garage, where he’d hidden the red car, started it up, then sat behind the wheel, thinking. Once already, in the name of goodness, he’d sullied himself with murder. Shouldn’t he at least try to kill this new, even more evil, premier? Otherwise, what had it all been about?Killing the new premier would entail killing another set of unlucky diners. For him: more panic attacks, fresh nightmares. This time, if he succeeded, he would at least take some credit. Good God, yes, he would: no more silent suffering in anonymity. Afterward, he would climb up on the hood of his red car and, addressing the people, propose a new movement that would eschew violence and rule by justice and gentleness forever. Also firmness, of course. A merciful firmness the people would instantly respect.Or he could forget the whole thing, go back to being the man he’d been before the first killing: a frightened, passive nobody.This thought made him sicker than the thought of another round of screaming and crunching.He leaped out of the still running red car, threw the garage door open, and, feeling alive and decisive, stood blinking in the morning sunlight, readying himself for his task.

MFA.MFA005: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.
MFA.MFA021: Of course, the man thought bitterly, of course the second you killed one damned autocrat a new one popped up, like an inconvenient erection, to take his place. It was Saturday. The man was sitting in a car in his dead uncle’s garage, pretending to drive. He couldn’t actually drive because he wasn’t on the run. The on the run part was over. Now he was simply in hiding. It was Saturday, and he’d killed the old premier on Tuesday, and the new premier had come to power on Thursday, and already his administration had implemented a series of performance improvement plans for striking agricultural workers that relied heavily on murder, or, as state media called it, “right-sizing the population through proactively attritionary removal policies.” The man looked down at the car. It was red. Blood red. An egregious cliché. But of course blood was red. He, of all people, should know that: his nightmares were full of it. The man stared at the steering wheel. There were two choices, right or left. Right meant he kept his head down. It wouldn’t be all bad. Right might mean a job, a house, a wife, at least once it was safe to assume a new identity. Right meant fear but not danger. His stomach turned. Left meant killing the new guy. Left meant assassination wasn’t just something he had done; “assassin” would be something he was. It would mean going public. Producing soundbites. Practicing a firm, inspirational set of his jaw for the inevitable Wanted poster. The man leaped up, determined.
MFA.MFA001: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.
